newsitem.title: CANADA: Brothers charged in Canadian orphanage sex scandal.
newsitem.headline: Brothers charged in Canadian orphanage sex scandal.

text.p: Police on Tuesday said they charged six members of a Roman Catholic lay order with the sexual and physical abuse of orphans who had been under their care years ago.

The six Christian Brothers were charged with abusing 17 boys at the now defunct Mount Cashel orphanage in St John's between 1950 and 1964. The children were 10 to 15 years of age at the time of the alleged abuse.
The accused men, who ranged in age from 59 to 72, worked as teachers at the now closed orphanage. The charges ranged from indecent assault to buggery.

Police said extradition proceedings have begun against four of the Christian Brothers in the United States so that they could stand trial in Canada. A former Mount Cashel worker who was not a Christian Brother has also been charged.
The charges came four years after eight members of Christian Brothers at Mount Cashel were convicted of abusing children at Mount Cashel during the 1970s.

Police said the latest charges stem from an investigation that began in 1989 following complaints of abuse by former Mount Cashel residents. Police interviewed more than 800 former residents and followed up 100 allegations of abuse.

The Christian Brothers group has been liquidating assets in the face of a C$35 million ($26 million) lawsuit brought by the former residents against the order and the Newfoundland government. So far, only one victim has received financial compensation.
The outbreak of the child abuse scandal rocked this windswept Atlantic-coast province, seriously damaging the Catholic Church's standing in Newfoundland society.
In 1990, Newfoundland's Archbishop Alphonsus Penney resigned after a Catholic Church panel he established to look into the allegations concluded that he and the church were to blame.

The Newfoundland charges were not isolated incidents. Similar charges laid in the early 1990s against operators of several Catholic Church run orphanages in the province of Ontario also resulted in criminal convictions.
